n: In this lecture we review the poisons isolated by dialysis. According to the outline, we study mineral acids, alkalis and salts, and the methods of their isolation and analysis. Key words and terms: dialysis, mineral acids, alkalis and salts. In the DVSSM complex this topic is taught as lecture 9, and the outline runs like this.

t: Groups of poisons isolated by dialysis
n: The poisons isolated by dialysis are divided into three groups. The first group is mineral acids: sulphuric, nitric and hydrochloric acids. The second group is alkalis: sodium and potassium alkalis, that is, NaOH and KOH, and ammonia. The third group is certain salts: potassium chlorate, that is, Berthollet salt, and also nitrites and nitrates. Remember, these three groups are examined together by dialysis.

t: When is the examination carried out?
n: Examination by dialysis is not always carried out. It is carried out only when the judicial authorities issue a referral. There is another case: the expert starts the examination on his own initiative if he finds grounds in the materials of the circumstances of the case or the case history. The grounds may also lie in the distinctive features of the specimen itself or in the result of a preliminary examination. It should be known that these substances are not among the substances that must be detected in every case.

t: Why is it difficult to detect acid and alkali?
n: Why is it difficult to detect acid and alkali? Pure acids and alkalis are rapidly neutralised in the body, so they often cannot be detected. The sulphate and chloride ions formed by neutralisation, and the carbonates of alkali metals, are constituents of the body. That is, the ions found do not in themselves prove poisoning. The same idea is given in the DVSSM complex.

Now we turn to the physical evidence. As physical evidence, vomit, wash water and food remains are taken. Of the internal organs, the stomach, large and small intestine, gallbladder with liver, trachea and oesophagus are examined. In the first stage the specimen is soaked in water for 1-2 hours and then filtered. In this way the liquid for the subsequent dialysis is prepared.

In the second stage, dialysis is carried out to remove protein substances. Dialysis is carried out 4-5 times, each time for 4-6 hours. Then the combined liquid is evaporated on a water bath to 5-10 ml. The stages of isolation run in sequence as follows: soaking with water, filtration, dialysis, evaporation and, finally, examination for acid, alkali or salt.

The dialysis apparatus is set up as follows. For dialysis, a crystalliser of 2-3 litres is taken and purified water is poured into it. A long glass beaker with its bottom cut off, over which parchment paper is fitted, is lowered into the crystalliser. A mixture of the crushed biological specimen and purified water is placed in the beaker. An important condition: the level of liquid in the beaker and in the crystalliser must be the same.

t: Detecting mineral acids with an indicator
n: In detecting mineral acids, an indicator is used first of all. A change in the colour of the indicator indicates the presence of mineral acids in the dialysate. The table lists four indicators: Congo red changes from red to blue, tropaeolin 00 from yellow to red, methyl violet to yellow-green, and dimethylaminoazobenzene to red. In addition, universal indicator paper may be used and pH measured with a potentiometer. An acidic medium shows the need to examine for particular acids.

t: Why one cannot test directly for anions
n: Why can the dialysate not be tested directly for anions? Direct testing of the dialysate for the anions SO4(2-), Cl- or NO3- is unsuitable. The reason is that these anions constantly enter with food substances, and some are formed in metabolism. Therefore, an acidic medium is first established with an indicator, then the acids are distilled off and the reactions are carried out only on the distillate.

The order of examination for acids is strictly fixed. First the strongest acid, that is, sulphuric acid, is examined, then nitric and hydrochloric acids. When sulphuric acid is found, hydrochloric and nitric acid may also be present in the dialysate, so the order is chosen this way. In the DVSSM complex the order is given in the same way.

We compare the LD50 values of the acids. For sulphuric acid the LD50 is 5-10 g. For concentrated, that is, 68 per cent, nitric acid the LD50 is 8-10 ml. For hydrochloric acid the LD50 is 10-20 g. As can be seen, the values are close to one another, but each acid is given in its own unit of measurement.

Toxicological significance of sulphuric acid. It is used in the chemical industry for obtaining fertilisers and in many fields, while being poisonous to the body. Its LD50 is 5-10 g. Poisoning depends on the concentration of the acid: even a 10-20% solution is considered poisonous to the body.

Signs of sulphuric acid poisoning. With concentrated acid, severe pain in the gastric tract, vomiting of blood and convulsions are observed. After a while the vomiting of blood stops, the abdomen is perforated, and the pain spreads over the whole abdominal cavity. Death occurs from incessant coughing and difficulty in breathing. On the corpse, dark patches are seen on the body, and the lips are grey and hard. Poisoning leads to death in more than 50% of cases.

The sequence of distilling sulphuric acid with copper. The concentrated dialysate is placed in the flask of the distillation apparatus, copper powder is added, and it is heated. A solution of iodine in potassium iodide is placed in the receiving flask. After the excess iodine has been removed in the receiving flask, reactions for SO4(2-) are carried out.

Three reactions are given for the sulphate ion. With BaCl2 a white precipitate forms, which is BaSO4. With Pb(NO3)2 a white precipitate also forms, which is PbSO4. The peculiarity of the second precipitate is that the PbSO4 precipitate dissolves in ammonium acetate and caustic alkalis. This property helps to confirm the reaction.

In the barium rhodizonate reaction, red barium rhodizonate is decolourised by sulphuric acid, that is, the red colour disappears. The amount of sulphuric acid is determined by the neutralisation method. In the DVSSM complex the reactions are given in the same order.

Toxicological significance of nitric acid. It is used in the chemical industry, in the synthesis of fertilisers, explosive nitrocellulose and drug substances. The LD50 of concentrated, that is, 68% nitric acid is 8-10 ml. This acid, besides hydrogen ions, also has an oxidising effect.

In nitric acid poisoning, acting on protein substances, the xanthoproteic reaction occurs: the tissue is coloured yellow. A yellow colour is seen on the lips, in the oral cavity and in the digestive tract. When the corpse is opened, a smell of nitrogen oxides comes from the internal organs, and in the stomach there are black areas due to haematin. In addition, methaemoglobin forms in the blood under the action of nitric acid.

Nitric acid is distilled with copper powder. In the reaction Cu(NO3)2, NO and water are formed; the equation is written as 3Cu + 8HNO3. The NO formed turns into NO2 in air. NO2 with water gives HNO3 and HNO2.

There are several reactions for nitric acid. With diphenylamine a blue colour forms. The azo dye formation reaction is also given. At high concentration it gives a yellow colour with wool, which turns brown under the action of ammonia. Concentrated sulphuric acid and brucine give a red colour with nitrates.

The toxicological significance of hydrochloric acid is explained by its use in various fields, including medicine. Its LD50 is 10-20 g. The signs of poisoning resemble those of sulphuric acid, only blackening of the organs is not observed. This difference is taken into account in distinguishing hydrochloric acid from sulphuric acid.

We compare the conditions for distilling the acids. With sulphuric acid, the concentrated dialysate is distilled with copper powder, the receiving flask contains a solution of iodine in KI, and the excess iodine is removed. Nitric acid is also distilled with copper powder, the reaction 3Cu + 8HNO3. With hydrochloric acid, the dialysate is distilled without copper powder, and the reactions are carried out on the distillate.

Reactions for hydrochloric acid. The dialysate is distilled without copper powder, and the reactions are carried out on the distillate. HCl gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate in an acidic medium, which is AgCl. With Berthollet salt free chlorine is released, and with potassium iodide and starch iodine is formed. The amount of hydrochloric acid is determined by the neutralisation method.

Now we turn to the alkalis. The alkalis of toxicological significance: caustic potassium, sodium and ammonia. Poisoning with other alkalis is rare. A strongly alkaline medium and a positive reaction for the corresponding metal cation indicate poisoning with alkali. An alkaline medium is determined by the change of phenolphthalein at pH 8-10.

Alkali must be distinguished from carbonate, because the colour of phenolphthalein changes in both alkali and carbonates. To the aqueous solution, 5% phenolphthalein is added, then BaCl2. If carbonate is present, a white precipitate of BaCO3 forms. If only alkali is present, there is no precipitate and the pink colour persists. With carbonate alone the precipitate is white and the colour disappears; if alkali and carbonate are together, the precipitate is white and the colour persists.

t: Isolation of alkalis from biological material
n: The procedure for isolating alkalis from biological material. The specimen under examination is crushed, distilled water is poured over it, it is left for 2-3 hours, then filtered. To the filtrate, 2-3 drops of alcoholic phenolphthalein solution are added. A red or pink colour indicates the presence of alkali or alkali metal carbonates. Then reactions for carbonates, for sodium and potassium cations and for ammonia are carried out. The amount is determined by the neutralisation method.

In identifying potassium hydroxide, the dialysate is first examined with indicators, as for sodium hydroxide. An alkaline medium, absence of carbonates and presence of the potassium ion indicate the presence of KOH. The reagents give a precipitate in a neutral or weakly acidic medium. Therefore the alkaline dialysate is neutralised or brought to pH 3-4 with acetic acid.

There are two main reactions for potassium. Sodium hydrogen tartrate in a neutral or acetic acid solution gives a white crystalline precipitate, which is KHC4H4O6. The precipitate dissolves well in hot water, mineral acids and alkalis. If the wall of the test tube is rubbed with a glass rod, the precipitate forms faster. Sodium cobaltinitrite, in turn, gives a yellow crystalline precipitate in a neutral or weakly acidic medium. This reagent must be freshly prepared.

In poisoning with sodium hydroxide, the dialysate has a distinctly alkaline medium and contains the sodium ion. The sodium ion is identified with potassium hydroxyantimonate and zinc uranyl acetate reagent. Hydroxyantimonate gives a white crystalline precipitate with sodium in a neutral or weakly alkaline medium. This reaction is interfered with by ammonium, magnesium and lithium ions.

The second reagent for sodium is zinc uranyl acetate. Neutral or acetic acid solutions of uranyl acetate give a green-yellow crystalline precipitate with sodium salts. The sensitivity of the reaction increases in the presence of zinc and magnesium ions. For this reason zinc uranyl acetate reagent is used in identifying sodium. Compared with hydroxyantimonate, which gives a white precipitate, here the precipitate is green-yellow.

We summarise the map for identifying alkalis. For potassium, sodium hydrogen tartrate and sodium cobaltinitrite are used; for sodium, hydroxyantimonate and zinc uranyl acetate. For ammonia, hydrogen sulphide is tested for first; then copper sulphate paper and Nessler reagent are used. Copper sulphate paper turns blue, and Nessler reagent gives a precipitate. In alkalis, the alkaline medium is determined with phenolphthalein at pH 8-10.

Finding ammonia does not always indicate poisoning. If the solution soaked with water contains the ammonium ion and a distinctly alkaline medium, this is grounds for saying poisoning with ammonia. However, finding ammonia in biological material does not always mean poisoning with that very preparation. Putrefaction of the organs of a corpse always forms a certain amount of ammonia; hydrogen sulphide is also formed.

Before testing for ammonia, one must test for hydrogen sulphide. If hydrogen sulphide is found, this indicates that putrefaction is under way, and testing for ammonia is not carried out. Method: 3-5 ml of solution is placed in a 50 ml flask and acidified with 10% HCl by litmus. A filter paper impregnated with lead acetate is hung under the stopper. If hydrogen sulphide is present, the filter paper blackens; this is PbS.

Reactions for detecting ammonia. 10-15 ml of solution is placed in a flask; moistened red litmus and filter paper impregnated with copper sulphate are hung under the stopper. Blue coloration of the papers indicates the formation of [Cu(NH3)4]SO4 and the presence of ammonia. Heating speeds up the colour change. Nessler reagent, in turn, gives a precipitate of dimercuriammonium iodide with an alkaline aqueous solution.

Now we turn to salts. Salts are isolated with the help of water: they belong to the method of isolating with water the substances of toxicological significance. These include nitrites, fluorides and chlorates. Of these, the ones of toxicological significance are the nitrites.

Toxicological significance of nitrites. Nitrites are used in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries; sodium nitrite is used in medicine to dilate vessels and as a preservative for sausages. Using them in place of table salt unknowingly leads to poisoning. Poisoning occurs mainly through the conversion of haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, and the blood turns chocolate-coloured. Signs: severe headache, reddening of the body, nausea, vomiting and strong dizziness.

t: Isolation of nitrites and the Griess reaction
n: Nitrites are isolated from biological material by soaking with water, and the filtrate is dialysed. Nitrites in the dialysate are identified in a neutral medium with diazotised sulfanilic acid and Griess reagent. Griess reagent consists of sulfanilic acid and naphthylamine; nitrites form an azo dye with it. The diazonium salt couples with phenol or amines in the para position; if it is occupied, in the ortho position.

Nitrites can also be identified with iodide-starch paper. 1% HCl and 3-4 drops of neutralised dialysate are dropped onto iodide-starch paper. If nitrite is present, the iodide-starch paper turns blue. The amount is determined by the photocolorimetric method on the basis of the azo dye formation reaction.

To conclude. The dialysis group includes mineral acids, alkalis, that is, NaOH, KOH and ammonia, and salts, that is, nitrite, nitrate and chlorate. Isolation is carried out by soaking, dialysis and evaporation; the acids are distilled off, and the order of examination is sulphuric, nitric, hydrochloric. For alkalis, phenolphthalein and BaCl2 are used, separate reactions are carried out for potassium and sodium ions, and ammonia is first tested for hydrogen sulphide. Nitrites are identified with Griess reagent and iodide-starch paper; the amounts of acids and alkalis are found by the neutralisation method.
